text: Richard Stallman is a computer scientist and software freedom activist born in 1953 in New York City. He had a troubled relationship with his parents and developed an early interest in computers, beginning with reading manuals at age 13. He attended Harvard University, where he excelled in mathematics, and later worked at MIT's AI Laboratory, where he became a prominent hacker and programmer. In the late 1970s, he became concerned about proprietary software restricting user freedom, leading him to found the GNU Project in 1983 with the goal of creating a free, open-source operating system compatible with Unix. He established the Free Software Foundation (FSF) to support the movement and pioneered the concept of copyleft, a licensing mechanism that ensures software remains free and modifiable. Stallman developed key GNU tools, including the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), GNU Emacs, and GNU Debugger. He also promoted free software principles through advocacy, public speaking, and the development of free software alternatives to proprietary systems. His activism extended to opposing software patents, digital rights management (DRM), and advocating for reduced copyright. He is known for his strong belief in user freedom, his criticism of commercial software, and his influence on the open-source movement. Stallman has received numerous honors, including the MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship, the Grace Murray Hopper Award, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Pioneer Award. He is widely recognized as a foundational figure in the free software movement and has been a vocal advocate for software freedom and ethical computing.
